title: Δῶρα καὶ πρέσβεις
titleEn: Agamemnon’s Offer and the Embassy — Iliad 9.114–204
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Agamemnon answers Nestor: he admits that he was bewildered and offers to make Achilles content. He names gifts that can be handed over at once (tripods, gold, cauldrons, prize horses, seven women of Lesbos, and Briseis returned with an oath that he never lay with her) and more for the day Troy falls: twenty Trojan women, one of his three daughters as a bride without bridal gifts, and seven towns as her dowry. All he asks is that Achilles yield, since he is the greater king and the elder. Nestor says the gifts can no longer be found fault with and names the envoys, Phoenix, Ajax and Odysseus with two heralds. After washing their hands and pouring a libation they walk along the shore, praying to Poseidon, and find Achilles singing to a lyre while Patroclus sits silent opposite. He welcomes them, seats them on purple carpets, and tells Patroclus to mix a stronger bowl.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Book 9 turns from Nestor’s speech, which ended at 113, to Agamemnon’s answer, and the edition’s paragraph begins here. The line is the formula for a speaker who answers in turn: τὸν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπεν the Homeric form of ‘addressed’ (Attic προσεῖπεν). The English keeps it apart from ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, which is a different formula. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον οὔ τι ψεῦδος ἐμὰς ἄτας κατέλεξας·
sentences.tr: ō geron ou ti pseudos emas atas katelexas·
sentences.l: “Old man, not at all a falsehood my bewilderments have you recounted;
sentences.i: “Old man, you have recounted my bewilderments, and not falsely;
sentences.n: Agamemnon accepts Nestor’s reproach at once. ὦ γέρον is ‘Old man’, the polite address to an elder; κατέλεξας is the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount, tell in order’, and ἐμὰς ἄτας ‘my bewilderments’ is its object. ἄτη is the clouded state of mind and the ruin it brings, and the plural most likely means the separate occasions of it. οὔ τι ψεῦδος is ‘not at all a falsehood’, with ψεῦδος used like an adverb, ‘untruly’; that is the usual explanation.

sentences.t: ἀασάμην, οὐδ’ αὐτὸς ἀναίνομαι.
sentences.tr: aasamēn, oud’ autos anainomai.
sentences.l: I was bewildered, nor do I myself deny it.
sentences.i: I was bewildered, and I do not deny it myself.
sentences.n: He confesses in one word. ἀασάμην is the aorist middle of ἀάομαι ‘be bewildered, be blinded in mind’, the verb that belongs with ἄτη in the line before, so the English keeps the echo: ‘bewildered’ beside ‘bewilderments’. οὐδ’ αὐτὸς ἀναίνομαι is ‘nor do I myself refuse it’: ἀναίνομαι ‘refuse, deny’, and αὐτός ‘I myself’ stresses that it is he who says so.

sentences.t:
ἀντί νυ πολλῶν
λαῶν ἐστὶν ἀνὴρ ὅν τε Ζεὺς κῆρι φιλήσῃ,
ὡς νῦν τοῦτον ἔτισε, δάμασσε δὲ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
anti ny pollōn
laōn estin anēr hon te Zeus kēri philēsēi,
hōs nyn touton etise, damasse de laon Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
Equal to many
peoples is a man whom Zeus in his heart may love,
as now he has honoured this man and subdued the people of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: A man whom Zeus loves at heart is worth as much as many peoples, as he has now honoured this man and subdued the people of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Why the wrong matters: one man is worth a whole army if Zeus is on his side. ἀντί with the genitive λαῶν πολλῶν is ‘in exchange for, equal to many peoples’, and νυ is a weak particle (‘then’) that the English leaves out. ὅν τε Ζεὺς κῆρι φιλήσῃ is ‘whom Zeus may love in his heart’: κῆρι is the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’, and the subjunctive with τε states a general case. The proof is the last clause. ὡς νῦν τοῦτον ἔτισε is ‘as now he has honoured this man’, Achilles, still unnamed (ἔτισε is the aorist of τίω ‘honour’), and δάμασσε ‘subdued’ is the aorist of δαμάζω with the doubled σσ that the metre allows.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἀασάμην φρεσὶ λευγαλέῃσι πιθήσας,
ἂψ ἐθέλω ἀρέσαι δόμεναί τ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα.
sentences.tr:
all’ epei aasamēn phresi leugaleēisi pithēsas,
aps ethelō aresai domenai t’ apereisi’ apoina.
sentences.l:
But since I was bewildered, having obeyed pitiful wits,
back I wish to make him content and to give unstinted ransom.
sentences.i: But since I was bewildered and obeyed my pitiful wits, I wish to make him content again and to give an unstinted ransom.
sentences.n: From confession to offer. ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἀασάμην repeats the verb of 116. φρεσὶ λευγαλέῃσι πιθήσας is ‘having obeyed pitiful wits’: φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν ‘wits’, λευγαλέος ‘pitiful’ (the wits led him wrong), and πιθήσας the aorist participle of πιθέω ‘obey’, the epic form beside πείθομαι, taking the dative. ἂψ is ‘back, again’: he wants to undo the deed. ἀρέσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀρέσκω ‘please, satisfy’; the Greek has no object, and ‘him’ is Achilles, as in the ‘make him content’ of 112. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι ‘give’, ἀπερείσι’ is ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’, and ἄποινα, the word for a ransom paid for a captive, is here compensation for a wrong.

sentences.t:
ὑμῖν δ’ ἐν πάντεσσι περικλυτὰ δῶρ’ ὀνομήνω
ἕπτ’ ἀπύρους τρίποδας, δέκα δὲ χρυσοῖο τάλαντα,
αἴθωνας δὲ λέβητας ἐείκοσι, δώδεκα δ’ ἵππους
πηγοὺς ἀθλοφόρους, οἳ ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο.
sentences.tr:
hymin d’ en pantessi periklyta dōr’ onomēnō
hept’ apyrous tripodas, deka de chrysoio talanta,
aithōnas de lebētas eeikosi, dōdeka d’ hippous
pēgous athlophorous, hoi aethlia possin aronto.
sentences.l:
And to you, among all, very famous gifts I will name:
seven unfired tripods, and ten talents of gold,
and fire-bright cauldrons, twenty, and twelve horses,
strong-packed, prize-bearing, which contest-prizes with their feet won.
sentences.i: And before you all I will name very famous gifts: seven unfired tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty fire-bright cauldrons, and twelve sturdy, prize-bearing horses, which have won prizes in contests with their feet.
sentences.n: The first list of gifts, one sentence over four lines, each item in the accusative. ὀνομήνω is an aorist subjunctive of ὀνομαίνω ‘name’ used like a future, ὑμῖν ἐν πάντεσσι ‘to you, among all’, and περικλυτά ‘very famous’ has περι- as ‘very’. Then ἕπτ’ ἀπύρους τρίποδας ‘seven unfired tripods’ (ἄπυρος: never yet set on a fire), τάλαντα ‘talents’ (a weight of gold), αἴθωνας … λέβητας ‘fire-bright cauldrons’. The twelve horses are πηγοὺς ἀθλοφόρους: πηγός is probably ‘firm, strong’, from πήγνυμι ‘make firm’, but the sense is not certain, and ἀθλοφόρος is ‘prize-bearing’. οἳ ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο is ‘which won contest-prizes with their feet’ (ἄροντο, aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’).

sentences.t:
οὔ κεν ἀλήϊος εἴη ἀνὴρ ᾧ τόσσα γένοιτο,
οὐδέ κεν ἀκτήμων ἐριτίμοιο χρυσοῖο,
ὅσσά μοι ἠνείκαντο ἀέθλια μώνυχες ἵπποι.
sentences.tr:
ou ken alēïos eiē anēr hōi tossa genoito,
oude ken aktēmōn eritimoio chrysoio,
hossa moi ēneikanto aethlia mōnyches hippoi.
sentences.l:
He would not be without a field of grain, a man to whom so much might come,
nor would he lack possessions of much-honoured gold,
as many contest-prizes as the solid-hoofed horses carried off for me.
sentences.i: A man to whom as much should come as my solid-hoofed horses have won me in prizes would be neither without a field of grain nor lacking in much-honoured gold.
sentences.n: A boast that tells the hearers what the horses are worth. οὔ κεν … εἴη is a potential optative, ‘would not be’. ἀλήϊος is ‘without grain-land’ (ἀ- + λήϊον ‘standing crop’), the usual explanation; ἀκτήμων is ‘without possessions’, with the genitive ἐριτίμοιο χρυσοῖο ‘of much-honoured gold’. ᾧ τόσσα γένοιτο … ὅσσα means ‘to whom as much should come as’, and ἠνείκαντο is the aorist middle of φέρω, ‘carried off’ as a winner does, with μοι ‘for me’. The point: a man who had won what these horses have won would be neither poor nor short of gold.

sentences.t:
δώσω δ’ ἑπτὰ γυναῖκας ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας
Λεσβίδας, ἃς ὅτε Λέσβον ἐϋκτιμένην ἕλεν αὐτὸς
ἐξελόμην, αἳ κάλλει ἐνίκων φῦλα γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
dōsō d’ hepta gynaikas amymona erga iduias
Lesbidas, has hote Lesbon eÿktimenēn helen autos
exelomēn, hai kallei enikōn phyla gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
I will give seven women, knowing blameless works,
Lesbian women, whom when well-built Lesbos he himself took,
I chose out for myself, who in beauty surpassed the tribes of women.
sentences.i: I will give seven women skilled in blameless crafts, women of Lesbos, whom I chose out for myself when he himself took well-settled Lesbos, women who surpassed the tribes of women in beauty.
sentences.n: Seven women are added. ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας is ‘knowing blameless works’ (ἰδυίας, feminine perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’; ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose real meaning is not known), the same words as in the Odyssey. Λεσβίδας is ‘women of Lesbos’. The subject of ἕλεν, a third-person aorist ‘took’ (Agamemnon himself would say ἕλον), can only be Achilles, the unnamed ‘him’ of the offer; αὐτός ‘he himself’ is set against ἐξελόμην ‘I chose out for myself’. So Achilles took the island and Agamemnon picked these women from the spoil. Line 129 ends on αὐτός with no stop, so it could also go with ἐξελόμην; the English takes it with ἕλεν. ἐϋκτιμένην is literally ‘well-built’, ‘well-settled’ in the free English; κάλλει ‘in beauty’, ἐνίκων ‘surpassed’, φῦλα ‘tribes’.

sentences.t:
τὰς μέν οἱ δώσω, μετὰ δ’ ἔσσεται ἣν τότ’ ἀπηύρων
κούρη Βρισῆος·
sentences.tr:
tas men hoi dōsō, meta d’ essetai hēn tot’ apēurōn
kourē Brisēos·
sentences.l:
These, on the one hand, to him I will give, and among them will be the one I then took away,
the girl of Briseus;
sentences.i: These I shall give him, and among them will be the one I took away then, the girl, the daughter of Briseus;
sentences.n: The women go back to Achilles, and with them the girl whom Agamemnon took. τὰς μέν ‘these, on the one hand’ are the seven women; οἱ is the dative ‘to him’; μετά is an adverb ‘among them’, and ἔσσεται is the epic future ‘will be’. ἣν τότ’ ἀπηύρων is ‘whom I then took away’ (ἀπηύρων, a first-person past of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’). κούρη Βρισῆος is ‘the girl of Briseus’: Briseis is named only by her father, not by her own name.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμοῦμαι
μή ποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι ἠδὲ μιγῆναι,
ἣ θέμις ἀνθρώπων πέλει ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
epi de megan horkon omoumai
mē pote tēs eunēs epibēmenai ēde migēnai,
hē themis anthrōpōn pelei andrōn ēde gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
and besides a great oath I shall swear
never to have set foot upon her bed, nor to have mingled with her,
as is the custom of human beings, of men and of women.
sentences.i: and I shall swear besides a great oath that I never mounted her bed or lay with her, as is the custom of human beings, men and women.
sentences.n: An oath that he has not touched Briseis. ἐπὶ δὲ … ὀμοῦμαι is a tmesis (a preverb standing apart from its verb), ‘and I shall swear in addition’, ὀμοῦμαι being the future of ὄμνυμι. μέγαν ὅρκον is ‘a great oath’, and its content is given by two aorist infinitives: μή ποτε … ἐπιβήμεναι (epic infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω, with the genitive τῆς εὐνῆς ‘her bed’) ἠδὲ μιγῆναι (aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, the usual verb of sexual union). The infinitives look back to what has already happened: ‘I never mounted her bed’. ἣ θέμις … πέλει is ‘as is the custom’ (πέλει = ἐστί), and ἀνθρώπων ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ γυναικῶν is ‘of human beings, of men and of women’.

sentences.t: ταῦτα μὲν αὐτίκα πάντα παρέσσεται·
sentences.tr: tauta men autika panta paressetai·
sentences.l: These things, on the one hand, at once all will be at hand;
sentences.i: All this will be at hand at once;
sentences.n: A pause between what is given now and what is promised for later. μέν ‘on the one hand’ is answered by the δέ of εἰ δέ κεν in the next unit, which turns to the time after the sack of Troy. παρέσσεται is the epic future of πάρειμι ‘be present, be at hand’, with σσ for σ; the gifts are on hand now.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν αὖτε
ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο θεοὶ δώωσ’ ἀλαπάξαι,
νῆα ἅλις χρυσοῦ καὶ χαλκοῦ νηησάσθω
εἰσελθών, ὅτε κεν δατεώμεθα ληΐδ’ Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
ei de ken aute
asty mega Priamoio theoi dōōs’ alapaxai,
nēa halis chrysou kai chalkou nēēsasthō
eiselthōn, hote ken dateōmetha lēïd’ Achaioi,
sentences.l:
and if, on the other hand,
the great town of Priam the gods should grant us to lay waste,
a ship with plenty of gold and bronze let him load for himself,
going in, when we divide the spoil, we Achaeans,
sentences.i: But if, on the other hand, the gods grant that we lay waste the great town of Priam, let him go in and load a ship with plenty of gold and bronze, when we Achaeans divide the spoil,
sentences.n: The second promise depends on the fall of Troy, and the sentence runs on past this unit’s comma. αὖτε ‘on the other hand’ marks the shift from the gifts now to those later. εἰ … κεν with the subjunctive δώωσ’ (= δώωσι, from δίδωμι) means ‘if the gods should grant’, with the infinitive ἀλαπάξαι ‘to lay waste’. The main verb is the imperative νηησάσθω, aorist middle of νηέω ‘heap up, load’: ‘let him load for himself’ a ship (νῆα) with ἅλις χρυσοῦ καὶ χαλκοῦ ‘plenty of gold and bronze’. The subject is not named, but it is Achilles; εἰσελθών is ‘going in’, and the Greek does not say into what. ὅτε κεν δατεώμεθα is ‘when we divide’ (subjunctive of δατέομαι), and ληΐδ’ is ληΐδα ‘spoil’.

sentences.t:
Τρωϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐείκοσιν αὐτὸς ἑλέσθω,
αἴ κε μετ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην κάλλισται ἔωσιν.
sentences.tr:
Trōïadas de gynaikas eeikosin autos helesthō,
ai ke met’ Argeiēn Helenēn kallistai eōsin.
sentences.l:
and Trojan women, twenty, let him himself choose,
those who after Argive Helen may be the fairest.
sentences.i: and let him choose twenty Trojan women himself, those who may be the fairest after Argive Helen.
sentences.n: The same imperative sentence goes on. Τρωϊάδας … γυναῖκας is ‘Trojan women’, ἐείκοσιν ‘twenty’ (the epic form of εἴκοσι), and αὐτὸς ἑλέσθω ‘let him choose them himself’ (aorist middle imperative of αἱρέω): the choice is Achilles’, not Agamemnon’s. αἴ κε … ἔωσιν is a relative clause with the subjunctive (ἔωσιν = ὦσιν): ‘those who may be the fairest’. μετά with the accusative is ‘next after’, and κάλλισται is the superlative of καλός. Ἀργείην Ἑλένην is ‘Argive Helen’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν Ἄργος ἱκοίμεθ’ Ἀχαιϊκὸν οὖθαρ ἀρούρης
γαμβρός κέν μοι ἔοι·
sentences.tr:
ei de ken Argos hikoimeth’ Achaiïkon outhar arourēs
gambros ken moi eoi·
sentences.l:
And if to Argos we should come, the Achaean udder of the plough-land,
a son-in-law to me he would be;
sentences.i: And if we should come to Achaean Argos, the udder of the plough-land, he would be my son-in-law;
sentences.n: A third promise, of marriage. εἰ δέ κεν with the optative ἱκοίμεθ’ (ἱκοίμεθα) is ‘and if we should come’. Ἄργος Ἀχαιϊκόν is ‘Achaean Argos’, a land or region of the Achaeans; the name is used of more than one place, and this passage does not settle which is meant. οὖθαρ ἀρούρης ‘the udder of the plough-land’ is a figure for rich farmland and is kept. γαμβρός … ἔοι is ‘he would be a son-in-law’ (ἔοι, epic optative of εἰμί, = εἴη; μοι ‘to me’).

sentences.t:
τίσω δέ μιν ἶσον Ὀρέστῃ,
ὅς μοι τηλύγετος τρέφεται θαλίῃ ἔνι πολλῇ.
sentences.tr:
tisō de min ison Orestēi,
hos moi tēlygetos trephetai thaliēi eni pollēi.
sentences.l:
and I shall honour him equally with Orestes,
who to me, late-born, is being reared in much abundance.
sentences.i: and I shall honour him equally with Orestes, who is being reared for me, late-born, in great abundance.
sentences.n: He would treat Achilles like his own son. τίσω is the future of τίω ‘honour’ (the form could also be read as a future of τίνω ‘pay’, but ‘honour’ fits μιν … ἶσον Ὀρέστῃ, ‘him equally with Orestes’, ἶσον being the adverb ‘equally’ with the dative). Orestes is Agamemnon’s own son. ὅς μοι τηλύγετος τρέφεται: τηλύγετος is traditionally ‘late-born’ (its origin is not known), and τρέφεται is the passive ‘is being reared’, θαλίῃ ἔνι πολλῇ ‘in much abundance’ (ἔνι = ἐν, set after its noun).

sentences.t:
τρεῖς δέ μοί εἰσι θύγατρες ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ
Χρυσόθεμις καὶ Λαοδίκη καὶ Ἰφιάνασσα,
τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσι φίλην ἀνάεδνον ἀγέσθω
πρὸς οἶκον Πηλῆος·
sentences.tr:
treis de moi eisi thygatres eni megarōi eupēktōi
Chrysothemis kai Laodikē kai Iphianassa,
taōn hēn k’ ethelēisi philēn anaednon agesthō
pros oikon Pēlēos·
sentences.l:
And three to me are daughters in my well-framed hall,
Chrysothemis and Laodice and Iphianassa,
of these whichever he wishes, dear, without bridal gifts, let him lead
to the house of Peleus;
sentences.i: I have three daughters in my well-framed hall, Chrysothemis and Laodice and Iphianassa; whichever of them he wishes, let him take her home, dear and without bridal gifts, to the house of Peleus;
sentences.n: The daughters on offer; the sentence runs four lines and stops at the sense-pause after Peleus’ house. τρεῖς δέ μοί εἰσι θύγατρες is ‘and I have three daughters’ (θύγατρες, the epic nominative plural; Attic θυγατέρες), ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ ‘in a well-framed hall’. τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσι is ‘whichever of them he wishes’ (τάων, epic genitive plural; κε with the subjunctive). φίλην ἀνάεδνον is ‘dear, without bridal gifts’: ἀνάεδνος means ‘without ἕδνα’, the gifts a bridegroom gives, so he will have nothing to pay. ἀγέσθω is ‘let him lead (as his bride)’, and Πηλῆος is the epic genitive of Πηλεύς, Achilles’ father.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐπὶ μείλια δώσω
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσ’ οὔ πώ τις ἑῇ ἐπέδωκε θυγατρί·
sentences.tr:
egō d’ epi meilia dōsō
polla mal’, hoss’ ou pō tis heēi epedōke thygatri·
sentences.l:
and I, besides, will give dowry-gifts,
very many, such as no one yet to his own daughter has given in addition;
sentences.i: and I shall add a dowry of very many gifts, such as no man has yet given with his own daughter;
sentences.n: Besides the daughter, a dowry. ἐπὶ … δώσω is a tmesis, ‘I will give in addition’. μείλια are gifts that go with a bride, here given by her father; the root is that of μειλίσσω ‘soothe’, and ‘dowry’ is the usual explanation, not certain. πολλὰ μάλ’ is ‘very many’. ὅσσ’ οὔ πώ τις … ἐπέδωκε is ‘such as no one has yet given’ (ἐπέδωκε, aorist of ἐπιδίδωμι ‘give besides’), and ἑῇ θυγατρί is ‘to his own daughter’: ἑῇ is the possessive ὅς, ‘his own’, not the relative.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ δέ οἱ δώσω εὖ ναιόμενα πτολίεθρα
Καρδαμύλην Ἐνόπην τε καὶ Ἱρὴν ποιήεσσαν
Φηράς τε ζαθέας ἠδ’ Ἄνθειαν βαθύλειμον
καλήν τ’ Αἴπειαν καὶ Πήδασον ἀμπελόεσσαν.
sentences.tr:
hepta de hoi dōsō eu naiomena ptoliethra
Kardamylēn Enopēn te kai Hirēn poiēessan
Phēras te zatheas ēd’ Antheian bathyleimon
kalēn t’ Aipeian kai Pēdason ampeloessan.
sentences.l:
And seven to him I will give, well-inhabited citadels:
Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, grassy,
and Pherae, most holy, and Antheia, deep-meadowed,
and fine Aepeia and Pedasus, vine-clad.
sentences.i: And I shall give him seven well-inhabited citadels: Cardamyle, Enope, and grassy Hire, and most holy Pherae, and deep-meadowed Antheia, and fine Aepeia, and vine-clad Pedasus.
sentences.n: Seven towns, named in a list that ends at 152. ναιόμενα is the present passive participle of ναίω ‘dwell’, so εὖ ναιόμενα is ‘well-inhabited’, and πτολίεθρα is the Homeric word for ‘citadels, towns’. Most of the names carry a stock epithet: Ἱρὴν ποιήεσσαν ‘grassy Hire’, Φηράς … ζαθέας ‘most holy Pherae’ (a plural name), Ἄνθειαν βαθύλειμον ‘deep-meadowed Antheia’ (βαθύς ‘deep’ + λειμών ‘meadow’), καλὴν Αἴπειαν ‘fine Aepeia’, Πήδασον ἀμπελόεσσαν ‘vine-clad Pedasus’. Cardamyle and Enope have none.

sentences.t: πᾶσαι δ’ ἐγγὺς ἁλός, νέαται Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος·
sentences.tr: pasai d’ engys halos, neatai Pylou ēmathoentos·
sentences.l: and all near the sea, the furthest of sandy Pylos;
sentences.i: all of them are near the sea, at the farthest edge of sandy Pylos;
sentences.n: Where the seven towns lie. πᾶσαι ‘all of them’ stands for the seven; ἐγγὺς ἁλός is ‘near the sea’ (ἁλός, genitive of ἅλς). νέαται is the feminine plural of νέατος ‘furthest, last’, and with Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος ‘sandy Pylos’ the usual explanation is that they lie on its farthest edge; the sense is taken from the word and not stated more fully here. ἠμαθόεις ‘sandy’ is the stock epithet of Pylos.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄνδρες ναίουσι πολύρρηνες πολυβοῦται,
οἵ κέ ἑ δωτίνῃσι θεὸν ὣς τιμήσουσι
καί οἱ ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ λιπαρὰς τελέουσι θέμιστας.
sentences.tr:
en d’ andres naiousi polyrrēnes polyboutai,
hoi ke he dōtinēisi theon hōs timēsousi
kai hoi hypo skēptrōi liparas teleousi themistas.
sentences.l:
and in them men dwell, rich in sheep, rich in cattle,
who will honour him with gifts like a god,
and under his sceptre will fulfil sleek rules of right.
sentences.i: and in them live men rich in sheep and rich in cattle, who will honour him with gifts like a god, and under his sceptre will fulfil sleek rules of right.
sentences.n: What the people of those towns will do for their lord. ἐν δ’ is ‘and in them’ (ἐν as an adverb); πολύρρηνες πολυβοῦται are ‘rich in sheep, rich in cattle’. οἵ κέ ἑ … τιμήσουσι is ‘who will honour him’ (ἑ is the pronoun ‘him’), δωτίνῃσι ‘with gifts’, θεὸν ὣς ‘like a god’. καί οἱ ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ … τελέουσι is ‘and under his sceptre will carry out’ (τελέουσι, the uncontracted epic future of τελέω (Attic τελοῦσι)), the sceptre being the mark of rule. λιπαρὰς θέμιστας is ‘sleek rules of right’: θέμιστες are what custom lays down as right, and here they are most likely the dues paid to a king, with ‘sleek’ meaning rich; the exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t: ταῦτά κέ οἱ τελέσαιμι μεταλήξαντι χόλοιο.
sentences.tr: tauta ke hoi telesaimi metalēxanti choloio.
sentences.l: These things I would accomplish for him, who has ceased from anger.
sentences.i: I would accomplish all this for him once he has ceased from his anger.
sentences.n: He sums up the whole offer, and sets its condition. ταῦτά κέ οἱ τελέσαιμι is a potential optative, ‘I would accomplish these things for him’ (οἱ ‘for him’). The condition is in the participle μεταλήξαντι, the aorist of μεταλήγω ‘cease from’ with the genitive χόλοιο (epic -οιο) ‘of anger’, agreeing with οἱ: ‘for him who has ceased from anger’.

sentences.t: δμηθήτω·
sentences.tr: dmēthētō·
sentences.l: Let him be subdued;
sentences.i: Let him be subdued;
sentences.n: What Agamemnon demands in return, in a single word. δμηθήτω is the aorist passive imperative of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with the vowel dropped (δμη- for δαμη-): ‘let him be subdued’. It is the verb of δάμασσε at 118, and ἀδάμαστος ‘unsubdued’ comes in the next unit, in the same line.

sentences.t:
Ἀΐδης τοι ἀμείλιχος ἠδ’ ἀδάμαστος,
τοὔνεκα καί τε βροτοῖσι θεῶν ἔχθιστος ἁπάντων·
sentences.tr:
Aïdēs toi ameilichos ēd’ adamastos,
touneka kai te brotoisi theōn echthistos hapantōn·
sentences.l:
Hades, you see, is ungentle and unsubdued,
for that reason also to mortals most hateful of all the gods;
sentences.i: Hades, you see, is unrelenting and unsubdued, and for that reason he is the most hateful of all the gods to mortals;
sentences.n: Hades is the example of what does not yield, and so of what men hate. Ἀΐδης is Hades, the god of the dead; τοι is a particle, ‘you see’. ἀμείλιχος ‘ungentle, unrelenting’ is ἀ- + the root of μειλίσσω ‘soothe’, and ἀδάμαστος ‘unsubdued’ is ἀ- + the root of δαμάζω, the word δμηθήτω before it. τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘for that reason’; βροτοῖσι is the dative plural (epic -οισι) ‘to mortals’, giving those who hate him, and θεῶν ἔχθιστος ἁπάντων is ‘most hateful of all the gods’.

sentences.t:
καί μοι ὑποστήτω ὅσσον βασιλεύτερός εἰμι
ἠδ’ ὅσσον γενεῇ προγενέστερος εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
kai moi hypostētō hosson basileuteros eimi
ēd’ hosson geneēi progenesteros euchomai einai.
sentences.l:
and let him submit to me, in as far as more kingly I am
and in as far as in birth the elder I claim to be.”
sentences.i: and let him submit to me, in as far as I am the more kingly and in as far as I claim to be the elder in age.”
sentences.n: Two further claims on Achilles’ obedience; the speech ends here and Nestor answers at 162. ὑποστήτω is the aorist imperative of ὑφίστημι in its intransitive sense, ‘let him stand under, submit’. The reasons come in two ὅσσον clauses: βασιλεύτερος is the comparative of βασιλεύς, ‘more kingly’ (the superlative was used of Agamemnon at 69), and γενεῇ προγενέστερος is ‘elder in birth’, ‘the elder’. εὔχομαι followed by an infinitive is ‘I claim’ to be so.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: Nestor replies, and the edition’s paragraph begins here. The line is Nestor’s stock reply-formula, the same words as 4.317: τὸν ‘him’ (the article as a pronoun), ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘then answered’, and the name-epithet Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ ‘the Gerenian horseman Nestor’. The meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (a place-name, Gerenia in Messenia, or a word near γέρων ‘old man’); ἱππότα is the epic nominative of ἱππότης ‘horseman’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
δῶρα μὲν οὐκέτ’ ὀνοστὰ διδοῖς Ἀχιλῆϊ ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste anax andrōn Agamemnon
dōra men ouket’ onosta didois Achilēï anakti·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
gifts, on the one hand, no longer to be found fault with you give to lord Achilles;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, you are giving lord Achilles gifts that can no longer be found fault with;
sentences.n: Nestor’s verdict on the offer. The first line is his address, the same line as 2.434: Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’, κύδιστε ‘most glorious’ (the superlative of κῦδος ‘glory’), ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’. διδοῖς is the epic second person of δίδωμι (Attic δίδως). ὀνοστά is a verbal adjective of ὄνομαι ‘find fault with, disdain’, so δῶρα … οὐκέτ’ ὀνοστά is ‘gifts no longer to be found fault with’. Ἀχιλῆϊ ἄνακτι is the dative ‘to lord Achilles’, with ἄναξ as a title of respect.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετε κλητοὺς ὀτρύνομεν, οἵ κε τάχιστα
ἔλθωσ’ ἐς κλισίην Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος.
sentences.tr:
all’ agete klētous otrynomen, hoi ke tachista
elthōs’ es klisiēn Pēlēïadeō Achilēos.
sentences.l:
but come, let us urge summoned men, who as quickly as possible
may go to the hut of Peleus’-son Achilles.
sentences.i: But come, let us urge on men called to the task to go as quickly as they can to the hut of Peleus’ son Achilles.
sentences.n: Nestor’s plan: send a delegation. ἀλλ’ ἄγετε is ‘but come’, in the plural, to the chiefs. κλητούς is ‘summoned men’ (κλητός, from καλέω ‘call’), here men called out for the errand; ὀτρύνομεν is a subjunctive of urging, ‘let us urge on’. οἵ κε τάχιστα | ἔλθωσ’ is a relative clause of purpose, ‘who are to go as quickly as possible’ (ἔλθωσ’ = ἔλθωσι, aorist subjunctive). κλισίην Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος is ‘the hut of Peleus’-son Achilles’, with the patronymic in the epic genitive -εω.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε τοὺς ἂν ἐγὼ ἐπιόψομαι οἳ δὲ πιθέσθων.
sentences.tr: ei d’ age tous an egō epiopsomai hoi de pithesthōn.
sentences.l: But come, those whom I shall look over; and let them obey.
sentences.i: Come then: those whom I shall pick out; and let them obey.
sentences.n: Nestor reserves the choice of men to himself. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is the idiom ‘but come’. The Greek has no main verb for τοὺς ἂν ἐγὼ ἐπιόψομαι ‘those whom I shall look over’, i.e. pick out (ἂν = κε; ἐπιόψομαι belongs to ἐφοράω ‘look upon’ and is future in form, though with ἂν it works like a subjunctive), so the English leaves the gap as the Greek does. οἳ δὲ πιθέσθων is ‘and let them obey’: οἵ is the demonstrative ‘they’, and πιθέσθων is the aorist middle imperative of πείθομαι ‘obey’.

sentences.t:
Φοῖνιξ μὲν πρώτιστα Διῒ φίλος ἡγησάσθω,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ Αἴας τε μέγας καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
Phoinix men prōtista Diï philos hēgēsasthō,
autar epeit’ Aias te megas kai dios Odysseus·
sentences.l:
Phoenix, on the one hand, first of all, dear to Zeus, let him lead,
but then Ajax, great, and heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: Let Phoenix, dear to Zeus, lead first of all, and then great Ajax and heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.n: The envoys are named, in order. Φοῖνιξ … Διῒ φίλος is ‘Phoenix, dear to Zeus’ (Διῒ, the dative of Ζεύς), and ἡγησάσθω is the aorist middle imperative of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’. The μέν waits for αὐτάρ ‘but then’ in the second line, which brings Αἴας … μέγας ‘great Ajax’ and δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’ (δῖος, the stock epithet); the verb ‘lead’ or ‘follow’ is understood. Ajax is called only ‘great’, and the passage does not say which Ajax is meant.

sentences.t: κηρύκων δ’ Ὀδίος τε καὶ Εὐρυβάτης ἅμ’ ἑπέσθων.
sentences.tr: kērykōn d’ Odios te kai Eurybatēs ham’ hepesthōn.
sentences.l: and of the heralds Odius and Eurybates together let them follow.
sentences.i: and of the heralds let Odius and Eurybates go along with them.
sentences.n: Two heralds are added. κηρύκων δ’ is partitive, ‘and of the heralds’, with Ὀδίος τε καὶ Εὐρυβάτης ‘Odius and Eurybates’ as subjects; ἅμ’ ἑπέσθων is ‘together let them follow’ (ἅμ’ = ἅμα; ἑπέσθων is the aorist middle imperative of ἕπομαι, third person plural). This Odius shares his name with a Halizonian leader met earlier in the poem, who was killed in Book 5 and so must be another man.

sentences.t:
φέρτε δὲ χερσὶν ὕδωρ, εὐφημῆσαί τε κέλεσθε,
ὄφρα Διὶ Κρονίδῃ ἀρησόμεθ’, αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ.
sentences.tr:
pherte de chersin hydōr, euphēmēsai te kelesthe,
ophra Dii Kronidēi arēsometh’, ai k’ eleēsēi.
sentences.l:
and bring water for the hands, and bid them keep holy silence,
so that to Zeus, the son-of-Cronus, we may pray, if he may take pity.”
sentences.i: and bring water for our hands, and bid them keep a holy silence, so that we may pray to Zeus, son of Cronus, in case he takes pity.”
sentences.n: The end of Nestor’s speech: wash, hush, pray. φέρτε is the second plural imperative of φέρω with the vowel dropped (Attic φέρετε), and χερσὶν ὕδωρ is ‘water for the hands’, to wash before praying. εὐφημῆσαι … κέλεσθε is ‘bid them keep holy silence’: εὐφημέω is to speak only words of good omen, which in a rite means to say nothing at all, and κέλεσθε is the present middle imperative of κέλομαι ‘command’. ὄφρα … ἀρησόμεθ’ is ‘so that we may pray’ (ὄφρα with the future of ἀράομαι), Διὶ Κρονίδῃ is the dative ‘to Zeus, son of Cronus’, and αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ is ‘in case he takes pity’ (ἐλεέω).

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῖσι δὲ πᾶσιν ἑαδότα μῦθον ἔειπεν.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, toisi de pasin headota mython eeipen.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and to them all a pleasing speech he uttered.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and what he said pleased them all.
sentences.n: The narrator reports how Nestor’s proposal was received; the edition’s paragraph begins here. ὣς φάτο is the speech-closing ‘so he spoke’. ἑαδότα is the perfect participle of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, so ἑαδότα μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘he spoke a pleasing word’ and τοῖσι … πᾶσιν ‘to them all’. The same line stands in the Odyssey (18.422, with ἔειπε), and the English follows it.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα κήρυκες μὲν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν,
κοῦροι δὲ κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο,
νώμησαν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπαρξάμενοι δεπάεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
autika kērykes men hydōr epi cheiras echeuan,
kouroi de krētēras epestepsanto potoio,
nōmēsan d’ ara pasin eparxamenoi depaessin.
sentences.l:
At once the heralds poured water over their hands,
and young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink,
and they dealt it out to all, having first poured drops into the cups.
sentences.i: At once the heralds poured water over their hands, young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink, and they served it out to all, first pouring a few drops into each cup.
sentences.n: The washing of hands and the first drink, in three clauses joined by μὲν … δὲ … δ’. Two of them are lines the poems use elsewhere: κοῦροι δὲ κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο is Odyssey 1.148, and νώμησαν … δεπάεσσιν is Iliad 1.471 and Odyssey 3.340. ἔχευαν is the aorist of χέω ‘pour’, ἐπεστέψαντο means they ‘filled to the brim’, and ἐπαρξάμενοι is the aorist participle ‘having first poured drops’, the first offering of the wine; δεπάεσσιν is the epic dative plural of δέπας ‘cup’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιόν θ’ ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
ὁρμῶντ’ ἐκ κλισίης Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο.
sentences.tr:
autar epei speisan t’ epion th’ hoson ēthele thymos,
hormōnt’ ek klisiēs Agamemnonos Atreïdao.
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
they set out from the hut of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, they set out from the hut of Agamemnon, son of Atreus.
sentences.n: The feast’s end and the envoys’ departure. The first line is a formula the Odyssey has (3.342 and 7.184): σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιόν θ’ is ‘poured libations and drank’ (aorists of σπένδω and πίνω), ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός ‘as much as the heart wished’. ὁρμῶντ’ is ὁρμῶντο, the imperfect middle of ὁρμάω ‘set out’, and the subject is the chosen envoys. Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο is ‘Agamemnon, son of Atreus’, the patronymic in the epic genitive -αο.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ
δενδίλλων ἐς ἕκαστον, Ὀδυσσῆϊ δὲ μάλιστα,
πειρᾶν ὡς πεπίθοιεν ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr:
toisi de poll’ epetelle Gerēnios hippota Nestōr
dendillōn es hekaston, Odyssēï de malista,
peiran hōs pepithoien amymona Pēleïōna.
sentences.l:
And to them many commands gave the Gerenian horseman Nestor,
casting glances at each, and to Odysseus most of all,
to try how they might persuade the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.i: And the Gerenian horseman Nestor laid many charges on them, casting glances at each, but on Odysseus most of all, to try how they might persuade the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.n: Nestor sends them off with instructions. πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε is ‘laid many charges’ (ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin’, imperfect), and Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ is his usual name-epithet. δενδίλλων ἐς ἕκαστον is ‘casting glances at each’, and Ὀδυσσῆϊ δὲ μάλιστα is the dative of the man charged (ἐπέτελλε is to be supplied again), ‘to Odysseus most of all’; δενδίλλω is a rare word, the usual explanation is ‘cast meaningful glances’, and the exact sense is not known. πειρᾶν is the infinitive of πειράω ‘try’, and ὡς πεπίθοιεν ‘how they might persuade’ is a reduplicated aorist optative of πείθω. ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the blameless son of Peleus’, Achilles; ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ βάτην παρὰ θῖνα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης
πολλὰ μάλ’ εὐχομένω γαιηόχῳ ἐννοσιγαίῳ
ῥηϊδίως πεπιθεῖν μεγάλας φρένας Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.tr:
tō de batēn para thina polyphloisboio thalassēs
polla mal’ euchomenō gaiēochōi ennosigaiōi
rhēïdiōs pepithein megalas phrenas Aiakidao.
sentences.l:
And the two went along the shore of the much-roaring sea,
very much praying to the earth-holder, the earth-shaker,
easily to persuade the great wits of the descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.i: And the two went along the shore of the loud-roaring sea, praying much to the earth-holder, the earth-shaker, that they might easily persuade the great mind of the descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.n: The envoys walk to Achilles’ camp, and the edition’s paragraph begins here. τὼ … βάτην is a dual, ‘the two went’ (βάτην, aorist dual of βαίνω without augment), and so is εὐχομένω ‘praying’; the dual means two men, and the passage names Odysseus as one of them (192) and does not name the other. παρὰ θῖνα is ‘along the shore’, and πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης ‘of the loud-roaring sea’. εὔχομαι here takes the dative of a god, so it is ‘pray’: γαιηόχῳ ἐννοσιγαίῳ, ‘to the earth-holder, the earth-shaker’, two epithets of Poseidon, whom the Greek does not name. ῥηϊδίως πεπιθεῖν is ‘to persuade easily’ (aorist infinitive of πείθω, reduplicated), and Αἰακίδαο is the patronymic ‘descendant of Aeacus’, a name for Achilles that goes back to his grandfather.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνων δ’ ἐπί τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἱκέσθην,
τὸν δ’ εὗρον φρένα τερπόμενον φόρμιγγι λιγείῃ
καλῇ δαιδαλέῃ, ἐπὶ δ’ ἀργύρεον ζυγὸν ἦεν,
τὴν ἄρετ’ ἐξ ἐνάρων πόλιν Ἠετίωνος ὀλέσσας·
sentences.tr:
Myrmidonōn d’ epi te klisias kai nēas hikesthēn,
ton d’ heuron phrena terpomenon phormingi ligeiēi
kalēi daidaleēi, epi d’ argyreon zygon ēen,
tēn aret’ ex enarōn polin Ēetiōnos olessas·
sentences.l:
and to the huts and the ships of the Myrmidons they came,
and him they found delighting in mind with a clear-sounding lyre,
fine, wrought, and on it was a silver yoke,
which he took for himself from the spoils, having destroyed the city of Eetion;
sentences.i: and the two came to the huts and ships of the Myrmidons, and found him delighting his mind with a clear-sounding lyre, fine and finely wrought, with a silver cross-bar upon it, which he had taken from the spoils when he destroyed the city of Eetion;
sentences.n: They reach Achilles’ camp and find him. The first line, Μυρμιδόνων … ἱκέσθην ‘came to the huts and ships of the Myrmidons’, is a line the Iliad has at 1.328, with the dual ἱκέσθην. τὸν … εὗρον is ‘and him they found’ (the pronoun points ahead; Achilles is named only at 193), φρένα τερπόμενον ‘delighting in mind’. The instrument is a φόρμιγξ ‘lyre’, λιγείῃ ‘clear-sounding’, καλῇ δαιδαλέῃ ‘fine, wrought’. ἐπὶ δ’ ἀργύρεον ζυγὸν ἦεν is ‘and upon it was a silver yoke’ (ἐπί is an adverb, ἦεν = ἦν); the ζυγόν ‘yoke’ of a lyre is the cross-bar joining its two arms. τὴν ἄρετ’ is ‘which he took for himself’ (ἄρετο, aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win, take for oneself’), ἐξ ἐνάρων ‘from the spoils’, ὀλέσσας ‘having destroyed’, Ἠετίωνος ‘of Eetion’.

sentences.t: τῇ ὅ γε θυμὸν ἔτερπεν, ἄειδε δ’ ἄρα κλέα ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr: tēi ho ge thymon eterpen, aeide d’ ara klea andrōn.
sentences.l: With this he was delighting his heart, and he sang the glories of men.
sentences.i: With it he was delighting his heart, and he sang the glories of men.
sentences.n: What Achilles does with the lyre. τῇ is ‘with this’, the lyre; ὅ γε is ‘he’; θυμὸν ἔτερπεν is ‘was delighting his heart’ (imperfect of τέρπω); ἄειδε is ‘he sang’. κλέα ἀνδρῶν ‘the glories of men’ uses the uncontracted plural κλέα of κλέος, and the phrase is what a minstrel sings in the Odyssey (8.73): songs of heroes. Achilles, who has left the fighting, sings of the deeds of other men.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δέ οἱ οἶος ἐναντίος ἧστο σιωπῇ,
δέγμενος Αἰακίδην ὁπότε λήξειεν ἀείδων,
τὼ δὲ βάτην προτέρω, ἡγεῖτο δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
στὰν δὲ πρόσθ’ αὐτοῖο·
sentences.tr:
Patroklos de hoi oios enantios hēsto siōpēi,
degmenos Aiakidēn hopote lēxeien aeidōn,
tō de batēn proterō, hēgeito de dios Odysseus,
stan de prosth’ autoio·
sentences.l:
And Patroclus alone, opposite him, was sitting in silence,
waiting for the descendant of Aeacus, when he should cease singing,
and the two went farther forward, and heavenly Odysseus led,
and they stood before him himself;
sentences.i: And Patroclus alone sat opposite him in silence, waiting for the descendant of Aeacus to stop singing; and the two went farther forward, with heavenly Odysseus leading, and stood before him;
sentences.n: One long sentence, kept whole because it ends only at the ano teleia after στὰν δὲ πρόσθ’ αὐτοῖο. Πάτροκλος … οἶος ἐναντίος ἧστο is ‘Patroclus alone sat opposite’ (ἧστο, imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; οἱ ‘to him’ goes with ἐναντίος). δέγμενος is the participle of δέχομαι in the sense ‘wait for’, with Αἰακίδην, Achilles again, as object, and the optative λήξειεν marks an event expected from the past: ‘until he should cease’. τὼ δὲ βάτην προτέρω is ‘and the two went farther forward’, with ἡγεῖτο ‘led’ and δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’. στὰν is the aorist of ἵστημι without the augment, ‘they stood’, and αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive of αὐτός, ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ταφὼν δ’ ἀνόρουσεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
αὐτῇ σὺν φόρμιγγι λιπὼν ἕδος ἔνθα θάασσεν.
sentences.tr:
taphōn d’ anorousen Achilleus
autēi syn phormingi lipōn hedos entha thaassen.
sentences.l:
and amazed sprang up Achilles,
with the lyre itself, having left the seat where he had been sitting.
sentences.i: and Achilles sprang up in amazement, lyre and all, leaving the seat where he had been sitting.
sentences.n: Achilles is named here for the first time since the envoys reached him. ταφών is the aorist participle of the verb that goes with τέθηπα ‘be astounded’ and τάφος ‘amazement’: ‘amazed’. ἀνόρουσεν is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’; αὐτῇ σὺν φόρμιγγι is ‘with the lyre itself’, he leaps up still holding it; ἕδος is ‘seat’, and θάασσεν the imperfect of θάσσω ‘sit’ without the augment.

sentences.t: ὣς δ’ αὔτως Πάτροκλος, ἐπεὶ ἴδε φῶτας, ἀνέστη.
sentences.tr: hōs d’ autōs Patroklos, epei ide phōtas, anestē.
sentences.l: And just so Patroclus, when he saw the men, stood up.
sentences.i: And in just the same way Patroclus, when he saw the men, stood up.
sentences.n: Patroclus does as Achilles did. ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and just so’, ‘in just the same way’ in the free English; ἐπεὶ ἴδε φῶτας is ‘when he saw the men’ (ἴδε is the aorist of ὁράω without the augment, φῶτας the accusative plural of φώς ‘man’), and ἀνέστη is ‘stood up’.

sentences.t: τὼ καὶ δεικνύμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tō kai deiknymenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: And to the two of them, gesturing, spoke swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: And gesturing a welcome, Achilles, swift of foot, said to the two of them:
sentences.n: The line introduces Achilles’ greeting; no one has just spoken to him, so it is not a reply-formula. The same words, with Menelaus as the speaker, stand in the Odyssey (4.59). τὼ is the dual ‘the two’ as object of προσέφη, and πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘Achilles, swift of foot’. δεικνύμενος is a participle of δείκνυμι ‘show, point’, so ‘gesturing’; the usual explanation for this place is that the gesture is one of welcome, but that sense is the lexicons’ and is not certain.

sentences.t: χαίρετον·
sentences.tr: chaireton·
sentences.l: “Welcome, you two;
sentences.i: “Welcome, you two;
sentences.n: Achilles’ first word. χαίρετον is the dual imperative of χαίρω ‘be glad’, used as the greeting on meeting someone, so ‘welcome’; the dual addresses the two envoys.

sentences.t:
ἦ φίλοι ἄνδρες ἱκάνετον ἦ τι μάλα χρεώ,
οἵ μοι σκυζομένῳ περ Ἀχαιῶν φίλτατοί ἐστον.
sentences.tr:
ē philoi andres hikaneton ē ti mala chreō,
hoi moi skyzomenōi per Achaiōn philtatoi eston.
sentences.l:
either dear men, you two, have come, or there is some great need,
you who to me, though I am sullen, of the Achaeans are the dearest.”
sentences.i: Either dear men have come, or there is some great need — you two who are, though I am sullen, the dearest of the Achaeans to me.”
sentences.n: Achilles guesses why they have come and says he is glad of them either way. ἦ … ἦ is ‘either … or’: ἱκάνετον, the dual of ἱκάνω ‘come’, ‘you two have come’, as φίλοι ἄνδρες ‘dear men’, or ἦ τι μάλα χρεώ ‘or there is some great need’ (χρεώ, epic ‘need’, with ἐστί left out). οἵ μοι σκυζομένῳ περ … is ‘you who, to me though I am sullen’: σκυζομένῳ ‘sullen’ (dative, agreeing with μοι), περ ‘although’, Ἀχαιῶν φίλτατοί ‘dearest of the Achaeans’ (partitive genitive, superlative of φίλος), and ἐστον ‘you two are’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας προτέρω ἄγε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
εἷσεν δ’ ἐν κλισμοῖσι τάπησί τε πορφυρέοισιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas proterō age dios Achilleus,
heisen d’ en klismoisi tapēsi te porphyreoisin.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, forward led heavenly Achilles,
and seated them on seats and on purple carpets.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and heavenly Achilles led them on farther in, and seated them on seats and on purple carpets.
sentences.n: He brings them in, and the edition’s paragraph begins here. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so then, having spoken’; προτέρω ἄγε is ‘led them farther in’ (ἄγε is the imperfect without the augment, = ἦγε, and the object is not expressed). εἷσεν is the aorist of ἵζω in its causing sense, ‘seated’. ἐν κλισμοῖσι is ‘on seats’ (κλισμός, a seat one could lean back in), and τάπησί τε πορφυρέοισιν ‘and purple carpets’ (the carpets are probably laid on the seats).

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Πάτροκλον προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.tr: aipsa de Patroklon prosephōneen engys eonta·
sentences.l: And at once to Patroclus he spoke, who was near:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke to Patroclus, who was near him:
sentences.n: Achilles gives Patroclus an order. προσεφώνεεν is the imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’, with the uncontracted -εε-, and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα is ‘who was near’ (ἐόντα, the accusative participle of εἰμί, agreeing with Πάτροκλον).

sentences.t:
μείζονα δὴ κρητῆρα Μενοιτίου υἱὲ καθίστα,
ζωρότερον δὲ κέραιε, δέπας δ’ ἔντυνον ἑκάστῳ·
sentences.tr:
meizona dē krētēra Menoitiou huie kathista,
zōroteron de keraie, depas d’ entynon hekastōi·
sentences.l:
“A larger mixing-bowl now, son of Menoetius, set up,
stronger mix it, and a cup make ready for each;
sentences.i: “Set up a larger mixing-bowl now, son of Menoetius, and mix it stronger, and make ready a cup for each;
sentences.n: Orders for the drink. μείζονα … κρητῆρα is ‘a larger mixing-bowl’ and καθίστα, an imperative of καθίστημι, is ‘set it up’; Μενοιτίου υἱέ is the vocative ‘son of Menoetius’, Patroclus. ζωρότερον is the comparative of ζωρός, whose usual explanation is ‘strong’, of wine, i.e. less watered; that sense is not certain, and another old guess is ‘warmer’. κέραιε is the imperative of κεραίω ‘mix’. δέπας δ’ ἔντυνον ἑκάστῳ is ‘and make ready a cup for each’ (ἔντυνον, imperative of ἐντύνω ‘make ready’).

sentences.t: οἳ γὰρ φίλτατοι ἄνδρες ἐμῷ ὑπέασι μελάθρῳ.
sentences.tr: hoi gar philtatoi andres emōi hypeasi melathrōi.
sentences.l: for those who are the dearest men are under my roof.”
sentences.i: for those who are under my roof are men most dear.”
sentences.n: His reason; this ends the speech. οἳ γάρ is ‘for those who’, the relative οἵ standing for ‘those’; φίλτατοι ἄνδρες ‘the dearest men’ (superlative of φίλος, as at 198). ὑπέασι is the epic third plural of ὑπεῖναι (ὑπό + εἰμί) ‘be under’, and ἐμῷ μελάθρῳ is ‘my roof’: μέλαθρον is the roof or roof-beam, here standing for the hut.
